Code on Prevention of Insider Trading
The Company has formulated and adopted a Policy in accordance 
with the requirements of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) 
Regulations, 2015, as amended. In compliance with the SEBI 
(Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, as amended, the 
Company has a robust Code of Conduct to prohibit and monitor 
insider trading in the Company, which is strictly followed within 
the Company and the reporting is done to the Audit Committee/ 
Board at regular intervals. The Policy lays down the guidelines 
and procedures to be followed, and disclosures to be made while 
dealing with the shares of the Company, along with consequences 
for violation. The policy is amended to bring it in line with the 
provisions of the prevailing regulations, from time to time.
Training programs were also conducted to spread awareness, 
and self-assessment tests were administered with a passing 
score. Further, the Company is working rigorously on effective compliance with SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 
2015, with all the amendments being discussed and their 
implementation within the stipulated time. Apart from training 
programs, one-o-one interactions and emails are sent to the 
officials for better understanding and clearance of any doubts. 
Pursuant to the provision of Regulation 3(5) and 3(6) of SEBI 
(Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 read with 
SEBI Circular issued in this regard and in view of Coforge Code of 
Conduct to regulate, monitor and report trading by designated 
persons (“Coforge PIT Code”), the Company has put in place a 
Structured Digital Database System (SDD) in compliance with 
the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. Strict 
action was taken against officials who were found guilty during 
the year. The Audit Committee also reviews compliance with the 
regulations at the quarterly/annual meetings. Procedures have 
been established for Directors, officers, designated persons, and 
their relatives regarding trading in the Company’s securities. These 
procedures are regularly communicated to employees identified 
as insiders. In addition, insider trading awareness sessions are 
held for designated persons. Notifications about trading window 
closures, during which Directors and designated persons/insiders 
are not allowed to trade in the Company’s securities, are provided 
in advance. The company adopted a stringent penalty framework 
for any violations, and any policy violations are addressed and 
reported to SEBI/Stock Exchanges as required, if any.

Performance Evaluation
The Board completed the process of annual performance 
evaluation of the Board/Committee/members for the year. This 
exercise was intended to ensure an independent, confidential, 
transparent and comprehensive assessment of the performance 
of the Board, its members and its committees, with responses 
collected directly through the tool.
The evaluation methodology covered various aspects, including 
structured questionnaires on overall Board effectiveness, 
evaluation of the Chairperson, peer evaluation of individual 
Directors (including Independent and Executive Directors), and 
evaluation of the Board Committees. The assessment also covered 
areas relating to Board composition, governance practices, risk 
oversight, financial monitoring, ESG and sustainability focus, 
strategy formulation, succession planning, people management, 
the quality and timeliness of information flow, and the conduct 
of Board and Committee meetings, together with provision 
for qualitative feedback to support a comprehensive report 
highlighting areas of strength and improvement.The evaluation was conducted in accordance with Sections 134 
and 178 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 19 of the SEBI 
(Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015, for the financial year 2025 26. The results of the assessment 
were presented to the Chairperson and subsequently to the Board.
The Chairperson communicated the feedback to all the members 
and deliberated on the same.

 Conservation of Energy & Technology Absorption
  Environmental sustainability aims to enhance human life 
quality while minimizing strain on the Earth’s resources. It 
embodies the responsibility to conserve natural resources 
and safeguard global ecosystems for present and future 
well-being. Achieving this equilibrium between humans and 
the natural world involves living in a manner that doesn’t 
deplete resources. An unsustainable situation arises 
when natural resources are depleted faster than they can 
be replenished.
  At Coforge, we are committed to continuously improving 
our environmental performance. We have committed to 
become a Zero Carbon organization by 2040. To achieve 
our commitment, we have undertaken the following 
key initiatives:
Energy & Climate Action
• Our long-term emission targets have been verified by SBTi, 
supporting overall reduction in energy use and emissions.
• 100% conversion of our employee transport fleet from diesel/
petrol to CNG in NCR locations, with expansion to other locations 
of operations.

facility and Gold LEED ID+C certification for the Hyderabad 
facility from the USGBC.  New certification for the Pune and 
Recertification for Greater Noida campuses under the EBOM 
framework is currently underway.
• Certified with ISO 14001:2015 and ISO 45001:2018 to ensure 
compliance through periodic audits.
• In the process of ISO50001 certification (Energy Management 
System).
• Transition to refrigerants with low warming potential.
• Upgrading AC units to more efficient units compatible with 
refrigerants of low warming potential.
• Replaced the hot water system at the guest house in Greater 
Noida facility with an energy-efficient solar hot water system, 
reducing energy consumption.
• An energy-efficient VRV system has been installed at the guest 
house, allowing independent operation and avoiding the need 
to run the entire 628 TR chiller plant during off-peak times.
• All diesel generators at the Greater Noida campus are equipped 
with Retrofit Emission Control Device to treat exhaust air 
before release.
• Prioritizing the use of green products for new facilities and 
appropriate waste segregation during and post-construction 
phases in India.
Green IT
• The reduction of 224 units of 150 Ah batteries from the 
data center UPS that significantly minimized lead-acid 
battery waste.
• All e-waste is disposed of only through government-
approved recyclers.
• Repurposing and reusing nearly 2,000 repaired IT assets 
(laptops) that resulted in avoidance of over 380 tons CO2e.
Renewable Energy
• Greater Noida campus has been running on 100% green energy 
since November 2024, contributing 62% of Coforge’s total 
energy consumption in India.
• Utilizing rooftop areas at the campus for solar energy 
generation through a 75 KW solar plant, reducing carbon 
footprint and grid power consumption.
• Collaborating with regional government authorities in all 
areas where Coforge operates to secure renewable energy 
connections for facilities.Other Sustainability Initiatives
• Committing to making our offices free from single-use plastic, 
with plastic waste limited to packaging material and disposed 
of through authorized recyclers.
• Processing food and horticulture waste in-house for 
manure production.
• In FY26, the campus initiated several measures to reduce 
single-use plastics, including compostable garbage bags, 
reusable glass bottles, recyclable bottles, and elimination of 
plastic carry bags and food wraps in dining areas.
• Health, Safety & Environment training modules in India to instill 
sustainability concepts in employees’ routines and actions.
• Launched mandatory ESG training for all employees.
• The Greater Noida campus has reduced paper cup usage from 
6 million to 0.2 million annually, and in FY25, 6,295 kilograms of 
Type 1 and 2 paper were recycled into internal-use stationery.
• In the process of ISO20400 certification (Sustainable 
Procurement) to integrate sustainable practices across our 
supply chain.
• Ran an employee awareness campaign to encourage our people 
to adopt sustainable practices and use resources efficiently.

Coforge has executed a focused shift in its Data & AI strategy— from 
consultative, project-led engagements to a more industrialized 
portfolio of offerings that accelerates datadriven transformation 
at scale. The strategy, branded as “6+2”, encompasses six core 
Data Modernization offerings and two AIfocused accelerators, 
enabling clients to modernize their data foundations and make 
them AI-ready.
Core Data Modernization Offerings:
1.  Data Appliance Decommissioning:  We support enterprise 
clients in retiring legacy data appliances such as Teradata, 
Exadata, and Greenplum, migrating them to modern 
cloudnative platforms like Snowflake and Databricks—
driving cost efficiency, elasticity, and performance gains.
2.  Pipeline Modernization:  We help clients shift from 
legacy ETL tools like Informatica and Ab Initio to modern, 
scalable PySpark-based data pipelines, enabling faster 
data movement, better maintainability, and alignment with 
modern data engineering standards.
3.  Report Rationalization & Modernization:  We rationalize 
and modernize legacy reporting platforms such as Business 
Objects, transitioning enterprises to self-service analytics 
platforms like Power BI. This improves accessibility, reduces 
cost, and promotes data democratization.
4.  Database Stack Modernization:  Coforge assists clients in 
upgrading their legacy database ecosystems—migrating 
from platforms like Sybase to modern, open-source 
alternatives such as PostgreSQL, improving agility, 
scalability, and licensing flexibility.
5.  ML Model Modernization: We enable the migration of legacy 
machine learning models developed in R or SAS to modern 
frameworks like Python, TensorFlow, and Scala, improving 
model portability, automation, and integration with cloud-
native AI stacks.6.  Data Quality, Governance & Lineage Implementation:  To 
ensure long-term reliability and trust in data, we implement 
enterprise-grade data governance, quality management, 
and lineage systems aligned with modern platforms—critical 
for regulatory compliance and AI readiness.
With 2 AI Accelerators for Data Transformation
Data4AI:  This offer focuses on making enterprise data AIready 
by preparing large, siloed datasets for AI consumption. It includes 
the creation of enterprise feature stores and vector stores, 
enabling effective retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and ML 
training pipelines.
AI4Data:  We embed AI within the data modernization process 
itself, using GenAI to automate pipeline generation, suggest 
schema mappings, enhance data quality checks, and streamline 
governance tasks—reducing time-to-value and human effort.
Strategic Impact:  The “6+2” data strategy has positioned Coforge 
as a scaled, modernization-first partner capable of delivering 
repeatable, platform-led transformation in Data and AI. This

1. Exit legacy technology with minimal disruption

Details in respect of adequacy of internal controls 
and internal and statutory audits
Internal audit / Statutory audit and secretarial audit
The Board and the Audit Committee regard the observations and 
recommendations of the auditors as an important independent 
validation of information received from management regarding the Company’s operations and performance. The Board and 
the Audit Committee periodically review the findings and 
recommendations of the statutory and internal auditors and 
recommend corrective actions, wherever necessary.
The Company monitors and evaluates the effectiveness and 
adequacy of its internal control systems, including compliance 
with operating processes, accounting procedures and Company 
policies, based on audit findings. It has established both external 
and internal audit mechanisms, and the auditors are provided 
access to all relevant records and information. Based on the reports 
of the Internal Auditor, process owners undertake corrective 
actions in their respective areas, if any, thereby strengthening the 
control environment. The internal control framework is designed 
to support operational effectiveness and efficiency, safeguard 
assets, ensure reliable financial and non-financial reporting, and 
secure compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
The clearly defined policies and procedures, process automation, 
employee training and development, and an organisational 
structure that separates responsibilities help in maintaining 
integrity and reliability within the internal control systems of 
the company.
The Company has appointed an external firm as its Internal 
Auditor. The Internal Auditor operates independently and is 
responsible for assessing and enhancing the effectiveness of 
risk management, controls and governance processes. The 
Internal Auditor provides risk-based advice and insights aimed at 
supporting organisational value creation. Annual audit plans are 
developed based on risk assessments, and comprehensive reviews 
are undertaken covering financial, operational and compliance 
controls. Where specialised knowledge is required, external 
experts are consulted or professionals with the relevant skills 
are engaged. Process improvements identified during reviews 
are communicated to management on a regular basis. The Audit 
Committee of the Board monitors the performance of the Internal 
Auditor through periodic review of audit plans, findings and the 
status of issue resolution. The Audit Committee meets at least 
four times a year to review internal audit findings. Separate 
review meetings of the Audit Committee Chairperson with the 
internal and statutory auditors are also held before quarterly 
meetings to enhance transparency and governance. In addition, 
the Audit Committee meets the Statutory Auditors during the 
year without the presence of management. Independent Directors 
also meet periodically without management to discuss important 
governance matters, and their recommendations are acted upon 
as part of the Company’s governance practices.
Statutory audit
Each financial year, the statutory and independent auditors 
confirm their independence and compliance with the relevant 
ethical standards. Based on the procedures performed, no risks or 
circumstances have been identified that could compromise their 
independence as auditors of the Company under the applicable 
Indian regulations.
The statutory and independent auditors examine whether the 
Company’s financial statements present a true and fair view of 
its financial position and performance. They conduct the audit in accordance with the applicable standards, review internal 
controls as considered necessary, and share their observations 
with management. These observations are discussed at the Audit 
Committee meetings, where the auditors’ recommendations, if 
any, are considered and appropriate actions are tracked and 
reported in subsequent meetings.
Similarly, secretarial audit forms an integral part of these audits. 
All the required information is supplied to the auditors within 
the stipulated time frame, with regular review meetings, and 
the quarterly reports are presented to the Audit committee for 
its noting.

Our global network of agile learning academies employs curated,

continuous employee development. This is facilitated through 
diverse learning methods such as anytime-anywhere solutions, 
Action Learning Projects, sandbox environments, benchmarks & 
assessments, virtual and blended programs, e-learning platforms,

strong workforce.
Xcellerate is our AI -enabled internal talent marketplace designed 
to proactively address skill gaps by mapping demand to precise Role 
Skill Combinations (RSCs). Leveraging the AI -enabled Xcellerate 
Competency Framework and Internal Talent Marketplace, Coforge 
provides deep visibility into skills, role expectations, and career 
trajectories - empowering employees to navigate their growth 
with precision. The platform features a scalable and customized 
inventory of skills and certifications, facilitating continuous 
workforce development through targeted training, certification 
programs, and real-time self -development resources. Xcellerate 
identifies technical, functional, and behavioral skills for each role, 
assesses current capabilities, and drives focused upskilling and 
reskilling initiatives.
The framework encompasses over 800 unique RSCs linked 
to 1200+ skills and behavioral competencies with associated 
learning pathways.
iEnable  is Coforge’s central learning ecosystem for technical, 
functional, and domain capability development. It works closely 
with the business to deliver role specific, future ready learning 
solutions, ensuring our 30,000+ workforce remains competitive 
in an evolving technology landscape. The platform supports 
upskilling, cross skilling, leadership development, and professional 
certifications across the organization.

My Voice - Employee Engagement Survey FY2026
Coforge utilizes its annual “My Voice” Employee Satisfaction Survey 
to gather actionable insights into engagement and satisfaction, 
directly informing workplace environment enhancements.
The FY26 “My Voice” survey recorded an overall participation rate 
of 82%, reflecting strong employee engagement and continued 
willingness to share feedback. The Satisfaction and Commitment 
Scores were both at 78%, providing valuable insights into employee 
sentiment and helping identify focused areas for strengthening 
the overall employee experience.
The FY26 “My Voice” EES identified key engagement drivers as 
Basic Needs (88%), Teamwork (86%), Company Brand & Image (80%), 
Training (80%), Manager Support (79%), and Communications (79%).

Prevention of Sexual Harassment of Women at the 
Workplace
The Company has a policy on Prevention of Sexual Harassment 
of Women at the workplace, in line with The Sexual Harassment 
of Women at the Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition & Redressal) 
Act, 2013. In accordance with the Act, Internal Complaints 
Committee (ICC) has been set up and contact details of ICC 
displayed prominently in all units of Coforge.The Company believes in providing all employees a congenial work 
atmosphere, which is free from discrimination and harassment, 
without regard to caste, religion, marital status, gender, sexual 
orientation, etc. During the year, the Company conducted various 
awareness programs and workshops at all locations. Employees 
are required to attend compulsory awareness and training 
program on POSH on our virtual learning platform – Percipio. 
Company has conducted orientation or training sessions for the 
ICC members and the HR team.
During the year 2025-26, three (3) complaints were reported, all of 
them were upheld and resolved; actions were taken in accordance 
with the POSH Act. There are no pending cases for action. The 
Company had duly resolved these complaints within 90 days in 
accordance with POSH Act.
Compliance with Maternity Benefit Act, 1961
The Company is compliant with the applicable provisions of 
the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and has policies, systems and 
processes in place to ensure ongoing compliance.

DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY
1.0 PREAMBLE:
1.1   This Policy (hereinafter referred to as the “Policy”) shall be 
called the “Dividend Distribution Policy” of Coforge Limited 
(hereinafter referred to as the “Company”).
1.2   The Policy has been framed specifically in compliance with 
the provisions of Regulation 43A of the Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 “Listing Regulations”.
1.3   Regulation 43A of the Listing Regulations mandates top 
1000 listed companies based on market capitalization to 
frame a policy for distribution of dividend.
1.4   This Policy aims at laying down a broad framework for 
considering decisions by the board of directors of the 
Company (“Board”), with regard to distribution of dividend to 
shareholders and/or retention or plough back of its profits.
2.0 POLICY
2.1   The dividend distribution shall be in accordance with 
the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, 
rules framed thereunder, the Listing Regulations and 
other legislations governing dividends and the Articles of 
Association of the Company, as in force and as amended from 
time to time.
 (a)  The circumstances under which the 
shareholders may or may not expect dividend;
   The Board determines and recommends dividend for 
a particular period after taking into consideration 
the financial performance of the Company and other 
parameters described in this Policy. The circumstances 
under which shareholders may not expect dividend are 
set out below:
  (i)  Proposed expansion plans requiring higher 
capital allocation;
  (ii)  Decision to undertake any acquisition(s), 
amalgamation(s), merger(s), joint venture(s), etc. 
which requires significant capital outflow;
  (iii)  Requirement of higher working capital for the 
purpose of business of the Company;
  (iv)  Utilization of surplus cash generated during the 
financial year in entirety for alternative forms of 
distribution such as buy-back of securities; or
  (v) In the event of loss or inadequacy of profit. (b)  The financial/internal factors that shall be 
considered by the Board before making any 
recommendations for a dividend include, but 
are not limited to:
  (i)  Reported and Projected Net Profit after Tax 
(PAT) and free cash flows, having regard to 
both standalone and consolidated financial 
performance for current and projected periods;
  (ii)  Operating cash flows and treasury position 
keeping in view the total debt to equity ratio.
  (iii)  Possibilities of alternate usage of cash, e.g. capital 
expenditure etc., with potential to create greater 
value for shareholders;
  (iv)  Providing for unforeseen events and 
contingencies with financial implications;
  (v) Dividend payout ratio and dividend yield;
 (c)  The external factors that shall be 
considered by the Board before making any 
recommendations for a dividend include,  
but are not limited to:
  (i)  Any significant changes in macro-economic 
environment affecting India or the geographies 
in which the Company operates, or the business 
of the Company or its clients;
  (ii)  Any political, tax and regulatory changes in the 
geographies in which the Company operates;
  (iii)  Any significant change in the business or 
technological environment resulting in the 
Company making significant investments to 
effect the necessary changes to its business 
model; or
  (iv)  Any changes in the competitive environment 
requiring significant investment.
 (d)  Policy as to how the retained earnings shall 
be utilized.
   Profits of the Company, to the extent not distributed as 
dividend, may be retained in the business and utilised 
by the Board, as it may determine from time to time, 
for any or more of the following purposes, including 
those outlined in Section 2.1(b) above:
  (i)  Capital expenditure and infrastructure 
investment to support organic growth;
  (ii)  Strategic acquisitions, mergers, joint ventures 
and investments;

Acquisition of Encora US Holdco, Inc. and Encora 
Holdings Limited
During the year under review, the Company entered into a Share 
Subscription and Share Purchase Agreement (“SSPA”) with Encora 
US Holdco, Inc. and Encora Holdings Limited (Cayman) (collectively, 
the “Target Companies”), Encora Holdco Limited (UK) and AI Altius 
Parent (Cayman) Limited (collectively, the “Investors”), in relation 
to the acquisition of shares of the Target Companies from the 
Investors, by way of a share swap arrangement. Pursuant to the 
SSPA, the Company proposed to acquire the Target Companies by 
issuance of equity shares of the Company as consideration other 
than cash.In accordance with the SSPA, the Company proposed to create, 
issue, offer and allot 9,37,96,508 (Nine Crore Thirty Seven Lakh 
Ninety Six Thousand Five Hundred and Eight) fully paid-up 
equity shares of face value INR 2 each at an issue price of INR 
1,815.91 per equity share, aggregating to a consideration of INR 
1,70,32,60,16,842. The proposed acquisition forms part of the 
Company’s strategic objective of expanding its global footprint 
and strengthening its digital engineering and technology 
services capabilities.
Issuance of Equity Shares on Preferential Basis 
pursuant to Share Swap Arrangement
The Board of Directors at its meeting held on December 26, 2025 
and the shareholders of the Company, through a postal ballot 
concluded on January 25, 2026, approved the issuance of equity 
shares on a preferential basis, on a private placement basis, as 
consideration other than cash under the share swap arrangement 
contemplated under the SSPA. The preferential issue involved 
issuance of up to 9,37,96,508 equity shares for an aggregate 
consideration of INR 1,70,32,60,16,842 to investors belonging to 
the non promoter category.
The preferential issue was approved in compliance with the 
applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, the rules made 
thereunder, Chapter V of the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2018, the Foreign Exchange 
Management (Non Debt Instrument) Rules, 2019 and other 
applicable laws.
Increase in Authorised Share Capital and Alteration of 
Memorandum of Association
The Board of Directors and the shareholders of the Company, 
at their respective meetings held on December 26, 2025 and 
through postal ballot concluded on January 25, 2026, approved 
the increase in the authorised share capital of the Company from 
INR 77,00,00,000 to INR 1,02,00,00,000 by creation of additional 
equity shares of face value INR 2 each. Consequent to the increase, 
Clause V of the Memorandum of Association of the Company was 
altered suitably to reflect the revised authorised share capital.

Coforge - Corporate Social Responsibility FY 2026
We believe that growth and responsibility are not parallel paths—
but the same journey. As we accelerate growth, we are also 
scaling our investment in long term social infrastructure for the 
communities we are a part of. 
We believe that growth must be accelerated—and purpose must 
be scaled—to create enduring value for business, society and 
the planet.
Our CSR efforts are focused on two priority areas:
1.  Education & Skill Development - We want to help children 
and adults from all backgrounds gain access to quality 
education, resources and skill development programs. 
2.  Environment & Sustainability-  We are committed 
to protecting local ecosystems and promoting 
sustainable practices through education, awareness, and 
community support.
Education & Skill Development: 
Key education partnerships and outcomes:
1.  The Coforge Public Library i s  o u r  fl a g s h i p  i n i t i a t i v e  t o  
democratize access to knowledge—creating inclusive, 
welcoming spaces that encourage lifelong learning for 
everyone, from infants and schoolchildren to senior citizens.
2.  Each Coforge Public Library is a thoughtfully designed 
space spanning 12,000–15,000 sq. ft., with comfortable 
seating, abundant natural light, and air-conditioning. Ramps, 
wide doorways, and spacious aisles ensure wheelchair 
accessibility. Each library houses a carefully curated 
collection of 12,000–16,000 books across a wide range 
of subjects, with a special focus on children’s literature. A 
dedicated children’s zone hosts storytelling sessions for 
young visitors. Never before has such infrastructure been 
made available to underprivileged communities.
  The entire catalogue is digitized, enabling visitors to locate 
books easily on digital screens placed near the entrance. 
Professionally trained and friendly librarians are always on 
hand to help.
  Unlike traditional libraries, we use a more browsing-friendly 
classification system and have painstakingly classified the 
entire collection in-house.
  All our libraries are free of charge and open from 9:00 a.m. 
to 8:00 p.m., seven days a week.
  The first Coforge Public Library in Noida was inaugurated on 
7 February 2024, followed by Gurugram on 7 June 2025 and 
Hyderabad on 7 October 2025. We plan to open at least four 
more libraries in Delhi NCR in FY27.
  The initiative has received an overwhelmingly positive 
response from across the community and won the CSR 
Initiative of the year in the Education category in FY26.   To date, the Noida Library has recorded a footfall of 66,763, 
Gurugram 57,785, and Hyderabad 43,126. What is even 
more heartening is that we have welcomed close to 2,500 
children from 84 government schools to our libraries while 
150 volunteers—drawn from Coforge employees and 
community members—have conducted reading programs in 
government schools, reaching 4,000 children. This impact is 
driven by a structured outreach program now active across 
all libraries: our librarians visit government schools within a 
5–7 km radius to engage principals and teachers and invite 
school visits; volunteers conduct reading sessions in schools 
and help coordinate student visits to the library. As most 
government schools do not have buses, we also arrange 
transportation. At the library, children are introduced to 
the full range of books and encouraged to explore topics 
of interest, followed by lively read-aloud sessions. Through 
these efforts, we aim to spark curiosity, strengthen literacy 
outcomes, and nurture a lifelong relationship with reading.
  We are proud to be building a project that is visionary, 
inclusive, and measurable in its impact.
  One of the biggest challenges in setting up these libraries 
is securing high-quality, safe spaces that are accessible to 
families and school-going children. Going forward, we wish 
to explore private–public partnerships with government 
bodies to establish libraries in more underprivileged areas—
expanding our footprint and deepening our impact for 
children who need it most.
3.  Primary Education (Support to first generation 
learners) – Vidya & Child
  Coforge has a long running partnership with Vidya & Child 
who run three schools for children who are first-generation 
leaners, in other words – children whose parents have not 
been to school. In FY26, 600 children across two government 
primary schools benefited from Coforge support. 
  These schools place emphasis on both foundational learning 
and aspiration building. 
  Apart from extending financial support, we arranged visits to 
The Coforge Public Library as well as to the Coforge Campus 
introducing young learners to professional environments 
and building their aspirations. Career awareness sessions 
led by senior leadership, offeried early insights into career 
pathways and the value of education while employee-led 
MS Office training, equipped children with basic digital and 
productivity skills to support future employability
4. Udayan Shalini Program – Girls’ Education
  Coforge continued its long-running partnership with the 
Udayan Shalini Program,  reaffirming its commitment to  
girls’ education. In FY26, we supported 190 girls  through 
the program, which provides academic and all-round support 
to deserving students from economically disadvantaged 
backgrounds—many of whom are at risk of dropping out due 
to social and financial constraints. The program encourages 
young women to aspire, persevere, and progress confidently 
toward higher education and employment.  Coforge leaders  conducted structured mentoring and 
enrichment sessions, offering guidance, life skills, and 
motivation. The Udayan Shalinis also visited The Coforge 
Public Libraries in Noida, Gurugram, and Hyderabad, 
strengthening their exposure to safe learning spaces and 
broadening their horizons.
5. Coforge Data & AI Lab, IIT (BHU) Varanasi:
  The Coforge Data & AI Lab at IIT (BHU), Varanasi was 
inaugurated on 23rd O c t  2 0 2 5  b y  B e t h  B o u c h e r ,  N o n -
Executive Director and Independent Director, and 
Chairperson of the Corporate Social Responsibility 
Committee, Anuradha Sehgal, Chief Brand & Sustainability 
Officer at Coforge and Prof. Amit Patra, Director, Indian 
Institute of Technology (BHU), Varanasi.
  The Coforge Data & AI Lab is a fantastic collaboration model 
where academic rigor meets industry expertise—bridging 
the gap between theory and enterprise-grade application. It 
will also contribute to research publications, open-source 
development,  and skill-building certifications  in emerging 
technologies such as cloud computing and machine learning.
  Speaking at the inauguration, Beth Boucher, Non-
Executive Director and Independent Director, and 
Chairperson of the Corporate Social Responsibility 
Committee, Coforge,  said:
  “We believe, AI will elevate human potential when guided by 
the right learning frameworks and responsible principles. 
The Coforge Data & AI Lab is designed to create new, high-
value roles in applied AI, data engineering, and intelligent 
automation, particularly in a country like India where scaling 
digital talent is both an opportunity and an obligation. By 
combining AI innovation with human learning and ethical 
transparency, the Coforge Data & AI Lab will be shaping 
a future where AI not only drives business value but also 
creates meaningful, inclusive, and sustainable employment 
opportunities for India and the world.”

  In FY 26, 2500 students, researchers, faculty members  
across multiple departments—including Computer 
Science, Metallurgy, Mathematics, Architecture, Electrical 
Engineering, Pharmaceuticals, and Engineering Physics 
benefited from the initiative. Students gained access to 
6,700+ curated Skillsoft digital courses, enabling self-
paced and continuous learning
  A structured cer tification pathway (On AI and Data Science) 
ensured depth and rigor through online foundational 
learning, faculty-led lectures and guided instruction, hands-
on capstone projects aligned to real-world applications. 
Masterclasses  were conducted by faculty and industry 
leaders on cutting-edge topics such as Agentic AI, robotics, 
healthcare AI, agriculture AI, image synthesis, recommender 
systems, and reinforcement learning
 The research projects being pursued at the lab include:
• AI-assisted vulnerability detection systems
• AI-powered assistive reading solutions for the 
visually impaired
• IoT- and AI-based soil health monitoring for 
sustainable agriculture
• Cognitive and brainwave-based interventions aimed at

6. Community Resource Center – Pune
  Coforge has partnered with CYDA to establish a Community 
Resource Center in Pune, focused on preparing youth for 
emerging job markets. In FY26, the Centre delivered STEM 
education programmes, foundational AI skills training, 
and career-readiness and employability support to 
300+ students.
7.  Women Entrepreneurship Program – Pune & Kolhapur
  Coforge has partnered with CYDA to run a women 
entrepreneurship program across Pune and Kolhapur. In 
FY26,  the program supported 100 women entrepreneurs 
with targeted training and seed capital and upskilled 300+ 
women  to enhance business resilience, financial literacy, 
and scalability.
  Coforge volunteers conducted skill building workshops for 
women, drawing on their own experiences to help them take 
steps towards financial independence and self reliability.
8.  Army welfare CSR Fund (Prabal Army Super 50, Pune)
  In FY26, Coforge was proud to extend its support to Prabal 
Army Super 50, a programme run by the Indian Army Welfare 
Fund to help children of soldiers and ex-servicemen who face 
financial constraints and cannot afford private coaching for 
competitive entrance examinations to higher-education 
institutions. Delivered in collaboration with knowledge 
partner Centre for Social Responsibility and Leadership 
(CSRL),  the programme operates across three centres—
Pune, Beas, and Mohali. It follows a rigorous merit-based 
selection process and trains 50 high-potential students  
at each centre every year. The fully residential programme 
significantly strengthens students’ prospects for higher 
education and future employment. Coforge sponsored the 
Pune centre.Environment & Sustainability
9. Surajpur Wetlands Restoration – Greater Noida
  Coforge, in partnership with GNIDA, is supporting the 
ecological restoration of the 308-hectare Surajpur Wetland 
in Greater Noida, including a 60-hectare  core waterbody 
that has been degraded by untreated wastewater inflows. 
We have appointed an on-ground implementation partner, 
Gurujal,  which brings expertise from similar restoration 
projects in Rajasthan  and Haryana. The project plan includes 
constructing a multi-drain system to treat wastewater 
before it enters the wetland.
 Expected outcomes include:
• Treatment of 64,735 MLD of wastewater
• 85% improvement in water quality
• Improved groundwater recharge
• Regeneration of biodiversity
• Community participation in ecosystem monitoring

10. Biodiversity Park & Green Belt Development
  A designated green area in Sector 108, Noida, had become 
a garbage dumping site. In August 2023, Coforge stepped 
in as a sponsor and cleared 22 truckloads  of waste. 
Nearly 500 Coforge employees then planted 10,000 
trees, transforming the area into a biodiversity park and a 
carbon-absorbing ecosystem. On 12 March 2026, Coforge 
volunteers from the Greater Noida campus returned to the 
site to plant 1,000 additional saplings.  Led by Coforge’s 
Chief Sustainability Officer, Anuradha Sehgal,  and the 
founder of “Give Me Trees”, Peepal Baba —a leading voice for 
afforestation in India—the volunteers planted native species 
such as Jamun, Peepal, and Arjun. The site was further 
enhanced with a water body to support birds, insects, 
and small animals, along with two insect hotels designed 
to aid insect survival. The initiative was appreciated by 
the local administration, with Mr. Anand Mohan,  Director 
(Horticulture), Noida Authority, also participating in the 
plantation drive.
11. Amrit Sarovar Rejuvenation
  Coforge continues to support the miantenance a pond 
rejuvenated last year in Sector…..,Noida which is now 
a thriving ecological space which supports hundred of 
migratory bird.
• Sustenance by 320,000 litres of treated sewage water
• Planned installation of a 2 0 KLD Wastewater Treatment 
Plant (WWTP)
• Deployment of floating treatment wetlands and bio-
enzymes
12. Citizen’s Park & Urban Greening
  Coforge adopted and revitalised a public park, a green belt, 
and traffic roundabouts in Greater Noida to strengthen 
urban green infrastructure. The enhanced green cover 
supports improved air quality and acts as a natural 
buffer against urban heat islands. In addition, rainwater-
harvesting pits were created along the green belt to reduce 
waterlogging during the monsoon and help recharge the 
groundwater table.
  The park redevelopment included an open-air gym, children’s 
swings, walking pathways, benches, and a gazebo, along with 
improved landscaping and fresh plantations. These upgrades 
have created a safer, more inviting community space for 
recreation and well-being, and the redevelopment efforts 
were widely appreciated by local residents.
13. Animal welfare
  The well-being of animals and the health of communities are 
closely linked. Supporting abandoned and injured animals—
alongside humane, scientific population management—helps 
reduce suffering, lower the risk of disease transmission, and 
create safer shared public spaces.
  In FY26, we supported four credible organisations—
Neighborhood Woof (Delhi), All Creatures Great and Small 
(Gurugram), Me and My Human (Faridabad), and Voice of 
Stray Dogs (Bengaluru).  Through these partnerships, we 
helped provide shelter, rescue support, and timely veterinary 
care for abandoned and injured animals, while also enabling 
humane stray dog population management through Animal 
Birth Control (ABC) and community awareness. Together, 
these interventions have contributed to cleaner and 
healthier neighbourhoods, improved public safety, and a 
more compassionate ecosystem where people and animals 
can coexist responsibly.
 Volunteering
  Coforge employees actively contribute time, skills, and 
leadership to advance the causes we support. Across 
education and skilling, volunteers mentor students, conduct 
career-awareness sessions, and deliver digital-skills training, 
while also engaging children through reading and storytelling 
as part of our library outreach. In our environmental 
initiatives, employees participate in on-ground plantation 
and restoration drives, and through our animal-welfare 
partnerships, they support community engagement that 
enables care, compassion, and responsible co-existence. 
Together, this culture of volunteering strengthens 
programme outcomes and deepens our connection with the 
communities we serve.Annual Report on CSR Activities

1. COFORGE PUBLIC LIBRARY, NOIDA 
Project Overview
As part of its CSR commitment towards education and community 
development, Coforge established the Coforge Public Library, 
Noida to provide free, high-quality access to books, learning 
resources, and reading spaces for all sections of society. The 
library aims to foster a culture of reading, improve access to 
knowledge, and create an inclusive community learning hub. 
Impact assessment was conducted by SoulAce Consulting using 
OECD-DAC evaluation principles. 
1. Project Snapshot
Particulars Details
Location Noida, Uttar Pradesh
Beneficiaries General public including students, 
professionals, senior citizens, 
families, and underserved children
Total Books Available 15,000+
Books Added in FY 2025-26 4,500
Languages English & Hindi
Library Footfall FY26 37,330
Student Outreach 120+ school visits reaching  
4,000+ children
2. Key Interventions
World-Class Public Reading Infrastructure
• State-of-the-art, fully air-conditioned library with 
comfortable seating.
• Technology-enabled catalogue search through kiosks and 
digital systems.
• Dedicated children’s reading zone.
• Professionally managed facilities and support staff.
• Free membership and book borrowing facilities. 
Reading Access for Underserved Children
• Organized visits for government and NGO schools.
• Free transportation provided to remove mobility barriers.
• Storytelling sessions and guided library orientations.
• Early exposure to books beyond school textbooks. 
3. Reach & Community Engagement
Strong and Growing Utilization
• Monthly visitor additions remained consistently high (2,600-
3,400 visitors/month).
• 41% users had been associated with the library for over three 
months, indicating sustained engagement.
• 31% were first-time visitors, demonstrating continued 
expansion of reach.Diverse User Base
• 43% students
• 36% working professionals
• Representation across genders and age groups, including senior 
citizens and homemakers.
• Library serves as a community space for learning, leisure, 
personal growth, and reflection. 
4. Key Impact Achieved
Improved Reading Habits
• 91%  of returning users reported improvement in reading habits.
• 90%  reported increased reading exposure, engagement, 
and curiosity.
• Users highlighted development of a consistent reading culture 
and greater exploration of diverse subjects. 
Enhanced Personal Growth & Confidence
• 76.8%  reported improved confidence, self-belief, and 
personal enrichment.
• Reading contributed to broader perspectives, motivation, and 
self-development across age groups.
• Professionals cited clearer thinking and learning, while senior 
citizens reported greater purpose and engagement
Expanded Educational Inclusion
• More than 4,000 underserved children  accessed books and 
library experiences through structured outreach.
• Many children reported their first-ever exposure to a 
professionally managed library.
• The program effectively reduced mobility and financial barriers 
to learning. 
High User Satisfaction
• 82% of respondents were extremely happy with the library.
• 93% appreciated the peaceful atmosphere.
• 96% appreciated comfortable seating.
• Users consistently rated ambience, facilities, staff support, and 
accessibility highly. 
5. Impact Across Multiple Levels
Individual Level
• Improved reading habits and knowledge acquisition.
• Enhanced confidence, motivation, and personal development.
• Increased engagement with books and lifelong learning.
Family Level
• Promoted reading as a shared household activity.
• Borrowed books frequently benefited multiple family members.
• Improved quality of family leisure time.Community Level
• Created an inclusive public learning and engagement space.
• Increased access to free, quality reading infrastructure.
• Strengthened reading culture among diverse community groups.
Systemic Impact
• Supports National Education Policy 2020 objectives.
• Strengthens public reading infrastructure in urban 
Uttar Pradesh.
• Demonstrates a scalable CSR-led model for literacy promotion 
and community learning. 
6. OECD-DAC Assessment Summary
Criteria Assessment
Relevance Highly relevant to community need for free 
reading infrastructure
Effectiveness Strong evidence of improved reading habits, 
engagement, and satisfaction
Impact Significant educational, social, and 
community outcomes
Efficiency High-quality services delivered free of cost 
with efficient resource utilization
Sustainability Strong long-term viability through Coforge 
support, growing membership, and 
community ownership
Conclusion
The Coforge Public Library has emerged as a high-impact, 
sustainable CSR initiative  that successfully addresses the gap 
in free public reading infrastructure while fostering a culture 
of reading and lifelong learning. With 30,000+ annual visitors, 
15,000+ books, and outreach to 4,000+ underserved children,  
the library demonstrates strong community relevance, high 
user satisfaction, measurable improvements in reading habits, 
and meaningful educational and social outcomes. The initiative 
represents a scalable and sustainable model of CSR-led public 
knowledge infrastructure that contributes directly to educational 
inclusion, literacy promotion, and community development
2. COFORGE PUBLIC LIBRARY, GURUGRAM 
Project Overview
The Coforge Public Library, Gurugram was established to 
address the lack of free, child-friendly, and high-quality public 
reading infrastructure in a rapidly urbanizing city. Designed as a 
community-focused reading space, the library promotes reading 
habits, independent learning, and educational inclusion through 
curated collections, technology-enabled discovery systems, and 
structured school outreach.

The Coforge Biodiversity Park at Sector 108, Noida, developed by

2. Transformation Achieved
From Landfill to Living Ecosystem
• Site was an illegal dumping ground for municipal and

• It was rejuvenated as a biodiversity park by removing 22 
truckloads of waste and planting 10,000 native saplings.
• Additional 1,000 trees planted in March 2026  to strengthen 
canopy cover and biodiversity.
• Recognized by Noida Authority, which allocated an additional

3. Key Interventions
Ecological Restoration
• Dense native-species plantation model.

the site.
• Plantation includes ecologically significant species such as 
Neem, Peepal, Bargad, Jamun, Arjun, Shisham and Karanj.
• Bamboo fencing and iron channeling installed for protection. 
Biodiversity Enhancement
• Creation of a bird bathing pond.
• Pond rejuvenation to improve water retention and soil moisture.
• Installation of 2 insect hotels to support pollinators and 
beneficial insects.
• Seed collection and native species propagation initiatives.
• Bio-enzyme preparation using organic waste for soil enrichment 
and natural pest control.

increased by 352.7%, ensuring greater year-round 
water presence. 
Improved Water Security
• Greater retention of rainfall and runoff.
• Enhanced groundwater recharge potential.

throughout the year.

Improved Soil & Vegetation Health
• 12.38% increase in land area under optimal soil moisture

vegetation growth.
• NDMI analysis confirms healthier vegetation and improved 
canopy moisture conditions. Water Quality Improvements
Several parameters remain within safe or improving ranges:
• pH within acceptable ecological range.
• TDS reduced from 2107 mg/l to 1010 mg/l.
• Electrical Conductivity reduced from 3550 to 1471 µS/cm.
• Nitrate reduced from 6.2 mg/l to 1.2 mg/l.
• Fluoride, Sulphate, Chloride, Arsenic, SAR and RSC remained 
within acceptable limits.
Environmental Benefits

9. Udayan Shalini Fellowship (USF) Programme
1. Programme Overview
Coforge supported The Udayan Shalini Fellowship,  a holistic 
scholarship and mentoring programme supporting academically 
meritorious girls from low-income households who are at risk of 
discontinuing their education due to financial limitations.   The 
programme supports the selected girls from Class XI through 
graduation and professional courses,  combining financial 
assistance with mentoring, life skills, employability training, 
career guidance, family engagement, and community service to 
ensure educational continuity and long-term empowerment. 
Key Components
• Scholarship support (₹10,000-₹30,000 based on education 
level)
• NAT-based selection process (Need, Ambition, Talent)
• Personalized mentoring and counselling
• Career guidance and exposure
• Employability and job-readiness training
• Family engagement and counselling
• Community leadership through “Paying it Forward”
• Alumni and volunteer support network 
2. Beneficiaries: 190 academically meritorious girls  from 
economically disadvantaged families across 11 locations  (Baddi, 
Delhi, Faridabad, Gurugram, Haridwar, Kalol, Kurukshetra, Nashik, 
Phagwara, Panchkula and Vikarabad). Socio-Economic Background
• 49% families earning below ₹12,000/month
Academic Profile
• 72% scored above 80% in Class X
• 40% scored above 90%
• Majority beneficiaries aged 18-19 years (52%) 
Assessment Conclusion:  The programme is successfully reaching 
academically meritorious girls at risk of discontinuing their 
education due to financial constraints. 
3. Key Outcomes & Impact
A. Educational Access & Continuity
Financial Support
• 71% received scholarships between ₹10,000-15,000
• 18% received ₹25,000-30,000 for professional courses
• 45% reported they could not have continued education 
without the scholarship
Impact
• 79% reported significant improvement in continuation 
of education
• Substantially reduced risk of dropout among beneficiaries. 
B. Academic Performance
• 100% reported improvement in academic performance
• 74% reported significant improvement
• Mentoring support contributed to improved subject 
understanding and academic confidence. Impact
The programme has successfully enabled girls to sustain education 
and perform better academically despite economic constraints. 
C. Mentoring, Confidence & Career Clarity
Mentoring Effectiveness
• 100% reported academic improvement due to mentoring
• Mentors matched with beneficiaries based on career interests. 
Personal Development
• 99% reported increased confidence and decision-
making ability
• 78% reported significant increase in confidence
• 97% demonstrated improved clarity regarding career and 
educational goals 
Impact
The structured mentor-mentee ecosystem is a key driver of 
confidence, career aspiration, and personal transformation. D. Employability & Workforce Readiness
Impact
• 96% reported improvement in employability and 
skill preparedness
• Strong foundation created for future workforce participation 
and career success. 
E. Family Engagement
Parent Participation
• 78% parents participated in workshops/counselling
• Families demonstrated stronger commitment towards 
girls’ education. 
Outcomes
• Improved understanding of academic and career goals (49%)
• Greater emotional and motivational support
• Increased family encouragement for higher education. 
4. Impact Across Multiple Levels
Individual Level
• Improved academic performance
• Higher confidence and decision-making ability
• Stronger employability and career readiness
• Increased educational continuity. 
Family Level
• Enhanced parental support
• Improved understanding of academic and career pathways
• Reduced financial burden on households
Community Level
• Increased volunteerism and civic engagement
• Fellows emerging as role models
• Positive influence on attitudes towards girls’ education. 
Systemic Impact
• Supports NEP 2020, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao
• Contributes to SDG 1, SDG 4, SDG 5, SDG 8 and SDG 10
• Promotes gender equity and access to higher education. 
5. OECD-DAC Evaluation
The programme received Very High ratings (5/5) 
across:  Relevance, Coherence, Effectiveness, Efficiency, 
Impact, Sustainability 
6. Key Conclusion
The assessment confirms that the Udayan Shalini Fellowship 
Programme is a highly effective and scalable model for 
educational empowerment of girls from disadvantaged 
backgrounds.  The integrated approach combining scholarships, 
mentoring, skills development, family engagement, and 
community service has generated significant improvements in 
academic performance, confidence, employability, career clarity, 
and educational continuity while fostering a generation of 
confident, socially responsible young women.

CORPORATE GOVERNANCE REPORT
At Coforge, our corporate governance practices are meticulously 
designed to prioritize shareholder interests while ensuring 
balanced consideration for all stakeholders in the absence 
of promoters. Our Board remains committed to protecting 
shareholder rights, fostering equitable treatment, and 
delivering value through ethical, legal, and sustainable decision-
making. By maintaining a strong and independent Board and 
adopting transparent accounting policies, Coforge ensures that 
shareholders have access to timely and credible disclosures, 
reinforcing trust and accountability.
The framework we employ aligns with domestic and international 
governance standards, providing shareholders with the 
assurance that their investments are managed responsibly and 
strategically. Through periodic compliance reports and continuous 
assessment of governance systems, internal and external audits 
our initiatives aim to uphold the highest standards of corporate 
integrity, safeguarding minority rights and amplifying long-term 
value creation.
Our corporate governance practices reflect our value system, 
encompassing our culture, policies, procedures, and genuine and 
long-term relationships with our stakeholders.
We believe that a shareholder-focused Board is integral to 
fostering trust and driving long-term value. By prioritizing the 
interests of all stakeholders, including minority shareholders, the 
Board ensures robust decision-making grounded in accountability 
and transparency. It actively works to safeguard shareholder 
rights, promoting equitable treatment and access to critical 
information. Through regular engagement, the Board cultivates 
an open dialogue with management, addressing concerns and 
integrating feedback into its strategic vision. This approach 
not only solidifies confidence in governance but also aligns the 
organization’s objectives with the expectations of its investors, 
thereby nurturing sustainable growth and enhancing value 
creation across the enterprise.
Integrity, accountability, fairness, ethics and transparency 
are key to our practices, ensuring we gain and retain the trust 
of our stakeholders from the beginning of our journey to the 
present. Corporate governance is about maximizing shareholder 
value legally, ethically, and sustainably. At Coforge, the Board 
exercises its fiduciary responsibilities in the broadest sense. Our 
disclosures aim to achieve the best practices in both domestic and 
international corporate governance. We also strive to enhance 
long-term shareholder value and respect minority rights in all our 
business decisions.
The Company’s approach to Corporate Governance aims to achieve 
the highest levels of transparency in accounting policies, a strong 
and independent Board, accountability, and equitable treatment in 
all facets of our operations. As a global organization, our practices 
align with emerging local and global standards and best practices. With this conviction, the Company has formulated procedures, 
policies, and systems to implement its corporate governance 
framework. The Company is in compliance with the Securities & 
Exchange Board of India (SEBI) corporate governance provisions 
stipulated under Regulation 34 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. The Company has 
been effectively complying with these provisions. The Company 
acknowledges that all our actions must serve the main goal of 
enhancing overall stakeholders value on a sustained basis.
The Company governs itself according to the fundamental principles 
of independence, accountability, responsibility, transparency, fair 
and timely disclosures, credibility, sustainability, etc., in all facets 
of its operations. These principles also serve as the means for 
implementing the philosophy of best corporate governance.
The management presents a quarterly status report on adherence 
to regulatory compliance to the Board of Directors. The Company’s 
governance standards are guided by the following principles:
• Excellence in corporate governance by abiding by guidelines 
and continuously assessing Board processes and management 
systems for constant improvement
• Greater attention to the protection of minority 
shareholders’ rights
The Company’s approach to Corporate Governance is founded on a 
rich legacy of fair, ethical, and transparent governance practices, 
which were in place even before they became mandatory. The 
Company is committed to good Corporate Governance, based on 
an effective Independent Board, the separation of supervisory 
roles from executive management, and the constitution of 
Committees to oversee critical areas. Good corporate governance 
requires a clear understanding of the respective roles of the Board 
of Directors and senior management and their relationships with 
others in management. The Company is committed to protecting 
the interests of all stakeholders and to maintaining high standards 
of values, ethics and business conduct. 
As part of a recent initiative and a risk management tool, the 
Company has implemented a comprehensive, robust, IT-enabled 
compliance management system for tracking, managing, and 
reporting on compliance with all applicable laws and regulations.

BOARD OF DIRECTORS
The Company is managed and controlled through a professional 
Board of Directors (“Board”) comprising of an optimum combination 
of Executive, Non-Executive and Independent Directors. The 
composition of the Board of the Company is in conformity with 
the provisions of the SEBI Listing Regulations & the Companies 
Act, 2013. The present composition of the Board is Nine (9) 
members out of which 5 (Independent) members are Independent 
Directors, constituting 55.56 percent of the total strength of the 
Board. The Board composition meets the requirement of at least 
one-half of the Board comprising of Independent Directors under 
Regulation 17(1)(b) of the SEBI Listing Regulations. The Chairman 
of the Board is Mr. O P Bhatt, who is Non-Executive Chairman. 
Ms. Beth Boucher serves as Independent Director and Ms. Shweta 
Jalan serves as a Non-Executive Non-Independent Director, both 
fulfilling the requirement of at least one woman director under 
Regulation 17(1)(a) of the SEBI Listing Regulations. As a global IT 
services company operating across multiple geographies, Coforge 
has a Board with diverse backgrounds and specialized expertise. 
Directors are appointed considering skills, experience and industry 
knowledge relevant to the Company’s business and governance 
needs. The brief profile of all the Directors is available on the 
website of the Company www.coforge.com.
Each Committee is supported by a dedicated working group or 
sub-committee that helps streamline the flow of information and coordinate review meetings with the respective Chairperson and 
other Board members, based on their queries and requirements. 
This process enables the Company to capture guidance, comments, 
and inputs in a timely manner and incorporate them appropriately 
before matters are presented to the full Board or the relevant 
Committee at the quarterly meetings. This structured approach 
strengthens governance, enhances transparency, and supports 
the Company’s effective functioning as a professionally 
managed organization.

Board by passing resolutions through circulation.Familiarization Program and Training for Independent Directors
The Company has a structured orientation and familiarization 
program for its newly appointed Directors and interactions with 
identified officials including CPO, CFO, CS are set up covering the 
nature of the Company’s business, its business model and its 
strategic and operating plans and key governance matters. The 
Director is also briefed on the Board and Committee’s functioning 
and the roles and responsibilities of its members. All Independent 
Directors have undergone this orientation at the time of their 
induction to the Board.
As part of ongoing training, the Company schedules quarterly 
meetings between Independent Directors and business and 
functional heads. These sessions include presentations on business 
models, new strategies and initiatives, risk mitigation measures, 
recent technology trends, changes in domestic and overseas 
industry conditions, digital transformation, developments in 
the global IT services industry, and the regulatory environment 
affecting the Company. The sessions also provide Independent 
Directors with a forum to share their views and suggestions on 
strategic and operational matters directly with the business and 
functional leadership teams. Details of the familiarization program 
are available on the Company’s website at www.coforge.com.
Succession Planning
The Company has established a robust succession planning 
framework to ensure orderly transitions across the Board, 
including Senior Management, and other executive roles. This is 
implemented by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee in 
coordination with the Board. At regular intervals, the Committee 
presents succession plans taking into account factors such as 
Directors’ tenure, performance evaluation outcomes, Board 
diversity, and business needs. In addition, the Company conducted 
a 360-degree review for Senior Management and other executive 
officers to maintain a leadership talent inventory and capability 
map, helping assess how effectively critical talent requirements 
align with business priorities.
The Board delegates the screening and selection process to the 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee. It presents a diverse 
slate of recommendations of eligible candidates to the Board for 
their approval as per the criteria laid down in the Nomination and 
Remuneration Policy. Subsequently, the Board recommends and 
places it before the shareholders for their approval.
Appointment Letters and Familiarization Program 
for Independent Directors
At the time of appointing an Independent Director (ID), a 
formal letter of appointment is given to him/her, which inter 
alia explains the role, function, duties and responsibilities 
expected of him/ her as an ID of the Company. The terms and 
conditions of the appointment are also placed on the website 
of the Company. All recently appointed Independent Directors 
were familiarized with the Company and its leadership in terms 
of the SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements), 
Regulations, 2015. The familiarization program also includes 
interactive sessions with business heads and senior leadership. 
The details of the familiarization program are available on the

Information flow to the Board
The Board receives information on an ongoing basis for review, 
input, and approval. It considers the Company’s annual strategic and 
operating plans, while quarterly and annual financial statements 
are reviewed first by the Audit Committee and then placed before 
the Board for approval. Matters such as business performance, 
appointment of Directors and Key Managerial Personnel, 
corporate actions, audit reviews, investor grievances, acquisitions, 
significant management decisions, material developments, risk 
management initiatives, legal matters, and statutory compliance 
are placed before the relevant Committees and, where required, 
submitted to the Board with their recommendations. Documents 
containing Unpublished Price Sensitive Information may, where 
necessary, be circulated to Board and Committee members at 
shorter notice in accordance with the Board’s general consent. 
As Directors are located across geographies, the Company 
provides video conferencing and other audio-visual facilities to 
support effective remote participation and decision-making. 
After each Board meeting, the Company tracks, reviews, and 
reports management action taken on decisions of the Board and 
its Committees.
The Company Secretary, in consultation with the Chairman, the 
CEO and the Executive Director, proposes the agenda for each 
meeting. The agenda, along with explanatory notes is circulated 
to the directors ahead of each meeting to facilitate informed 
deliberation and decision-making. Every Board member can 
suggest the inclusion of additional items in the agenda.
The Board meets at least once a quarter to review the quarterly 
results and other items on the agenda. Additional meetings are 
held when necessary. With the Board represented by directors 
from various parts of the world, it may not be possible for all 
of them to be physically present at every meeting. Hence, the 
Company provides video / teleconferencing facilities to enable 
their participation. Each member is expected to ensure their 
other commitments do not materially interfere with their 
responsibilities towards the Company.Actions to be taken after meetings
The management works on the decisions and suggestions made 
by the Board and its Committees. All actions are promptly 
communicated to the relevant departments or divisions. 
Status reports regarding action taken on prior decisions and 
recommendations are reviewed at subsequent meetings for 
further consideration and necessary actions.
Besides the committees mentioned, the company also reviews 
major risks, devises mitigation plans, and continuously 
monitors action item closures through discussion at global 
leadership meetings.

implications for the IT sector. Key trends highlighted included 
AI-driven emissions growth, increasing exposure to extreme 
weather risks, the expansion of green technology markets, and 
rapid shifts in workforce skill requirements. The training also 
covered the highlights of peer practices across sustainability 
solutions, inclusive hiring, employee development, and governance 
disclosures, emphasizing rising stakeholder expectations for 
transparent ESG reporting and demonstrable, verified outcomes. 
The training also covered updates on significant regulatory 
developments relevant for readiness planning, including the 
EU’s simplified CSRD requirements, emerging climate disclosure 
regulations in California and New York, India’s phased climate 
finance taxonomy, and SEBI’s revised timelines for BRSR value 
chain reporting.
To maintain this trust, continuous efforts are made to facilitate 
effective corporate governance measures, such as the 
constitution, governance, and working of Board committees.

The Committee supervises financial reporting processes to ensure accurate disclosure of financial statements, credibility, and compliance 
with Accounting Standards, Stock Exchanges, and other legal requirements. It reviews both internal and external audits and internal 
control systems to assess their adequacy and compliance. Additionally, it examines internal audit findings, oversees the Company’s

annual accounts.

in the subsidiary exceeding rupees 100 crore or 10% of the asset size of the subsidiary, whichever is lower, including existing loans/
advances/investments at the provision’s enforcement date. It reviews compliance with SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 
2015 and verifies that internal control systems are adequate and effective. The Committee acts as a link between Statutory and Internal 
Auditors and the Board of Directors. Governed by a Charter aligned with regulatory mandates under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI 
Listing Regulations (as amended), the Committee reviews information specified in Part C of Schedule II of SEBI Listing Regulations.

NOMINATION AND REMUNERATION POLICY
PREAMBLE
In terms of Section 178 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the 
Regulation 19 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India 
(Listing obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 
(“Listing Regulations” ), as amended from time to time, the Board 
of Directors of a listed company shall constitute the Nomination 
and Remuneration Committee ( “Committee” ) consisting of 
three or more Non-Executive Directors out of which at least 
two-third shall be Independent Directors and the Chairperson of 
the Committee shall be an Independent Director as well. Provided 
that the Chairperson of the Company, whether executive or non-
executive, may be appointed as a member of the Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee but shall not chair such Committee.
Further, the Committee is required to devise a policy to lay 
down a framework in relation to remuneration of Directors, 
Key Managerial Personnel and Senior Management Personnel. 
Accordingly, the Nomination & Remuneration Policy ( “Policy” ) of 
the Company has been formulated under the Companies Act, 2013 
and the Listing Regulations. This Policy shall also act as a guideline 
for determining, inter-alia, qualifications, positive attributes and 
independence of a Director, matters relating to appointment, 
removal and evaluation of performance of the Directors, Key 
Managerial Personnel and Senior Management Personnel..
(a) ROLE OF THE COMMITTEE
 This key role of the Committee is hereunder:
1)  To ensure that the level and composition of remuneration is 
appropriate to attract, retain and motivate directors of the 
quality required to run the Company successfully.
2)  To ensure that the relationship of remuneration 
to performance is clear and meets appropriate 
performance benchmarks.
3)  To lay down criteria with regard to identifying persons who 
are qualified to become Directors, Key Managerial positions 
and Senior Management Personnel and to determine their 
terms and remuneration including plans for succession for 
appointments to the Board (for Independent Directors, 
the committee will initiate the replacement process 
atleast 9 months in advance before end of tenure). For 
senior management:
 i. The committee will review the succession plan annually
 ii.  The committee will be updated on the key roles, as 
needed to align with overall growth strategy.
  a.  To formulate the criteria for evaluation of 
performance of Independent Directors and other 
Directors on the Board.
  b. To devise a policy on diversity of the Board.
  c.  To determine whether to extend or continue the 
term of appointment of an Independent Director, on the basis of the report of performance 
evaluation of Independent Directors.
  d.  To ensure that the remuneration to Directors, Key 
Managerial Personnel, and Senior management 
personnel of the Company involves a balance 
between fixed and incentivized pay, reflecting 
short and long-term performance objectives 
appropriate to the working of the Company and 
achievement of its goals.
  e.  Recommend to the board remuneration, payable 
to senior management Personnel
  f.  Formulation and administration the Company’s 
Employee Stock Option Programs from time 
to time
(b) MEETING AND QUORUM
  The Committee shall meet at least once in a financial year. 
A quorum of the Committee meeting shall be either two 
members or one-third of the members of the Committee 
whichever is greater, including one Independent Director 
in attendance. In case the Chairperson is not present at a 
Committee meeting, the members present at the meeting 
shall, amongst themselves, elect a Chairperson for that 
particular meeting.
(c) APPLICABILITY
  This policy is applicable to Directors (Executive, Non-
Executive and Independent), Key Managerial Personnel and 
Senior Management Personnel
(d) DEFINITIONS

(e)  APPOINTMENT AND REMOVAL OF DIRECTOR, KMP, 
SENIOR MANAGEMENT PERSONNEL
1) Appointment criteria and qualifications
 (i)  Subject to the applicable provisions of the Act, 
the Listing Regulations, other applicable laws, if 
any, and the Company’s Policy, the Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee shall identify and ascertain 
the integrity, qualification, expertise and experience 
of the person for appointment as Director, KMP or at 
Senior Management level and recommend to the Board 
his/her appointment and to recommend to the Board, 
plans and process for succession for appointments to 
the Board and senior management.
 (ii)  The Committee has discretion to decide the adequacy 
of qualification, expertise and experience for the 
concerned position.
 (iii)  The Company shall not appoint or continue the 
employment of any person as Managing Director/ 
Whole-time Director /Manager who has attained 
the age of seventy years, provided that the term of the person holding this position may be extended 
beyond the age of seventy years with the approval of 
shareholders by passing a special resolution.
 (iv)  The Company shall not appoint or continue the 
directorship of any person as Non-Executive Director 
who has attained the age of 75 years, unless a special 
resolution is passed to that effect, in which case the 
explanatory statement annexed to the Notice for such 
motion shall indicate the justification for appointing 
such person.
 (v)  A Whole-time KMP of the Company shall not hold office 
in more than one company except in its subsidiary 
company at the same time. However, a whole-time KMP 
can be appointed as a Director in any company, with the 
permission of the Board.
 (vi)  The Company shall not appoint any resigning 
Independent Director, as a Whole-time Director, unless 
a period of one year has elapsed from the date of 
resignation as an Independent Director.
2) Term/Tenure
 (i) Managing Director/Whole-time Director:
   The Company shall appoint or re-appoint any person as 
its Executive Chairman, Managing Director or Executive 
Director for a term not exceeding five years at a time. 
No reappointment shall be made earlier than one year 
before the expiry of term.
 (ii) Independent Director:
  (a)  No Independent Director shall hold office for more 
than two consecutive terms of up to maximum 
of 5 consecutive years each. Such Independent 
Director after completion of these two terms 
shall be eligible for appointment after expiry of 
three years of ceasing to become an Independent 
Director; provided that an Independent Director 
shall not, during the said period of three years, be 
appointed in or be associated with the Company 
in any other capacity, either directly or indirectly.
  (b)  The appointment of Independent Directors 
shall be made as per the provisions of the Act 
and Listing Regulations, as amended from time 
to time.
  (c)  At the time of appointment of Independent 
Director it should be ensured that the total 
number of Boards on which such an Independent 
Director serves is restricted to:
   (I)  seven listed companies as an Independent 
Director OR
   (II)  three listed companies as an Independent 
Director in case such a person is serving as a 
Whole-time Director of any listed Company.

Performance Evaluation
Pursuant to Sections 134 and 178 of the Companies Act, 2013 
and Regulation 19 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015, as amended from time to time, 
the Board carried out the annual performance evaluation of its 
own functioning, the performance of individual Directors, and the 
effectiveness of its Committees.
To support the evaluation, the Company engaged an independent 
Board advisory firm and used its secure digital evaluation 
platform. This enabled an independent, confidential, transparent, 
and comprehensive assessment of the performance of the Board, 
its members, and its Committees. Responses were collected 
directly by the external firm and shared with the Company only in 
aggregated and anonymised form.
The evaluation methodology included structured questionnaires 
developed under the supervision of the Chairperson of the 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee and the Board 
Chairperson. It comprised rating-based surveys covering 
overall Board effectiveness, evaluation of the Chairperson, peer 
evaluation of individual Directors—including Independent and 
Executive Directors—and assessment of Board Committees.
The assessment covered Board composition, governance practices, 
risk oversight, financial monitoring, ESG and sustainability focus, 
strategy formulation, succession planning, people management, 
the quality and timeliness of information flow, and the conduct 
of Board and Committee meetings. It also included open-ended 
qualitative feedback to help identify key strengths and areas 
for improvement.
The evaluation results were first presented to the Chairperson 
of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee and thereafter 
to the Board. The Chairperson shared the feedback with all Board
